title: The original Old Man Mose and the publishers' revamped version
summary: Randolph says his Old Man Mose verse began on the fifth in minor and the publishers rewrote it on the tonic; he notes he often had to go along with the program.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That's why Walter Winchell said both orchids to Louis Armstrong and his Orchestra, this time. This was not that bad, and they played the original Old Man Mose, and not the one that the publishers revamped and messed up.
Oh, what was that? I know Louis made a record in '35 in New York named Old Man Mose, and there was something --
It was from the piano sheet. See, he made a record, and also, Eddie Duchin made an arrangement on it, made a recording on it.
I remember, when I was a kid, seeing a movie short of -- first time I had ever seen Betty Hutton. She was still with Vincent Lopez' band.
Yes.
And that was the name of the short, Old Man Mose, and she came out jumping all over the place.
Yes.
Doing 'Old Man Mose.' Of course, at that time, I didn't know that you had written it.
Yes, uh-huh. Well, --
How did it differ from what you wrote, and from what was published?
Well, you've heard it. And you'd know it when you heard it, wouldn't you?
Yes.
Okay, now, it differs in this way -- in this respect. The verse of 'Old Man Mose' started on the fifth of the chord. It was a minor chord.
Uh-huh.
The publishers' arrangers took it and revamped it, and wrote the verse on the tonic. And when they come to the chorus, they still kept the tonic going. See, they kept that tonic going.
Uh-huh.
Which -- there wasn't any variety.
Yeah.

I don't know whether you know this young man or not, he's a very good arranger. His name is Kenneth Anderson. Kenneth said, -- he was down to one of the publishers downtown, and said to the fellow, picks up the arrangement, 'Old Man Mose, piano copy, say, Ken, here's a lousy tune. Ken say, you mean that score is a lousy score. Say, I
know the man that wrote the tune. Said, the tune itself is a very nice tune. But that score isn't the tune.
Couldyyou play it the way you originally wrote it?

I can play some of it. It's so long now. Now, for instance, like -- now, the publishers started it out this way: (Piano playing). When they get through going through all that, then they say, (Piano playing), see what I mean? But mine was different. (Piano playing.) I've forgotten part of it, though, now, because it's been so long since I've written it.
But then it jumps from that key, from this key -- (piano playing), one of those things, you see?
Yeah.
Well, so I had to just go along with the program.
You've said that several times during the interview, when things that you couldn't control, you just went along with them.
Yeah, just --
But that '34 band had that arrangement.
They had that arrangement, and they -- I wish you could have heard it. It was something beautiful to behold, not just that -- they say always you avoid a fellow that
sticks with the I's all the time.
What does that mean, reading?
That's the -- they say -- no, it's always said to avoid the -- avoid being with the guy that's always "I", --
Oh, like "me."
No, like me -- yeah, --
Yeah, that's what I mean.
Yeah, uh-huh.
The letter I.

Yeah, see, you stay away from, say, here comes Randolph. Yeah, he going to say "I so-and-so, I this, I the other," because they always stick -- but, you know, sometimes, when the truth is the light right, you've got to say "I".
That's right.
Yes. It's no use to saying nothing else, when it's the truth.
That's what Jelly Roll Morton used to say.
Yes.
I'm just telling you the truth.
